edges.relationship: Parr uses Bourdieu’s embodied history and habitus to explain how past practice persists in bodies and shapes later responses.
edges.evidence_note: Own Sensing Changes 8–9 explicitly uses Bourdieu to move beyond bodies being conditioned by circumstances: they also hold past practice outside conscious memory and influence later action. Page 9 names habitus with Mauss’s prior work; 12 groups Bourdieu with Hayles, Maturana, Varela, Connerton, Lefebvre and Merleau-Ponty rather than giving him sole credit. This is a particular conceptual resource for the six case studies, not formal mentorship or a complete reading of Bourdieu. Preview ends after 23, so endnotes 14, 16, 24 and 41 are unavailable; visible markers are not claimed as read notes.

edges.relationship: Parr draws on Cronon’s warning about narrative’s rhetorical razor to make ecological and bodily knowledge a priority for environmental history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 9–10 describes Cronon’s 1992 problem with linear narrative representing ecological nonlinearity and randomness, then explicitly agrees that these marginalized senses should be brought into environmental and technological history. Pages 13 and 20 reuse his caution and call to attend to autonomous nonhuman nature. This is Parr’s attributed reading and methodological use, not a claim that Cronon rejects all narrative or that she abandons language. She explicitly retains useful insights from literary scholarship on 8–9. Original Cronon works and absent endnotes 26/63 unread.

edges.relationship: Parr presents Corbin’s integrated histories of the sensing self as a model for recovering embodied knowledge of environments and technologies.
edges.evidence_note: Own 11 calls Corbin the leading practitioner of sensory history and explains his shift from individual senses to the seaside and Pinagot’s natural and social landscapes, emphasizing synaesthesia. She makes that recovery specifically valuable to her project and continues on 12 with the complex specificity of bodies. This is an explicit methodological exemplar, not proof of direct contact or independent validation of every reconstruction. Actual Corbin books and absent endnotes 33–36 unread.

edges.relationship: Parr uses Merchant’s contrasting accounts of Indigenous and Euro-American understandings of nature to develop her account of historically embodied environmental knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Own 19–20 gives Merchant’s interpretation of Native American forest gardening and regeneration alongside European Christian, scientific and capitalist conceptions of fallen nature. Parr uses this contrast to explain different bodily and epistemological relationships with environments before turning to Cronon and gender. These are Merchant’s broad historical interpretations as Parr employs them, not a newly certified uniform Indigenous worldview or a fresh reading of Merchant’s book. Original work and absent note 62 unread.

edges.relationship: Parr uses Lefebvre’s reciprocal relation between material and social bodies to describe how corporeal and symbolic embodiment can work together.
edges.evidence_note: Own 22 closes the introduction’s examples by saying the two modes often exist in tandem, then explicitly invokes Lefebvre’s reciprocal implication and explication. Page 23 makes recovering embodied histories the aim. The use qualifies a simple opposition between bodily knowledge and discourse; she does not discard social meaning. Lefebvre also appears in the jointly credited conceptual lineage on 12. This is a bounded conceptual resource, not a claim that his whole theory was adopted; original work and absent endnotes unread.

edges.relationship: Parr challenges the discursive account of the body she attributes to Foucault and grounds her environmental histories in embodied knowledge that can elude textual representation.
edges.evidence_note: Own 8 explicitly contrasts her assumptions with Foucault’s epistemological view of the body existing only in discourse. Pages 8–10 retain useful linguistic and literary insights while seeking material and sensory knowledge beyond them. This is Parr’s characterization and disagreement, not a finding that the complete Foucault corpus makes only that claim. The quoted formulation’s absent endnote 17 cannot be traced further from this preview, so no direct original quotation or source attribution beyond Parr is asserted.

edges.relationship: Parr argues that the symbolic account of embodiment she attributes to Butler needs to be supplemented by the gendered bodily experience of work and environments.
edges.evidence_note: Own 20 credits Butler’s insights in Gender Trouble and Bodies That Matter into power relations and the constraints gendered assumptions place on genetic research, then argues that gender is also made by active corporeal experience. Scott is explicitly credited alongside Butler; the criticism does not assert that all gender construction is false or that embodied differences are timeless biological essences. The title-specific discussion is Parr’s reading, with the complete originals and absent note 65 unread.

edges.relationship: Parr argues that Scott’s discursive account of gender should be supplemented by the bodily experience of historically different work and environments.
edges.evidence_note: Own 20 links Scott’s gender-as-a-category argument to the epistemological premises of Butler’s work, then states that gender is also made through active experience and corporeal embodiment. Pages 8–12 explain this supplement while retaining useful linguistic insights and historically specific bodies. This is a bounded later disagreement with equal Butler credit, compatible with the earlier Scott resource already 1683; no wholesale reversal, naturalized sex roles or rejection of gender history is inferred. Scott’s original article and absent note 66 unread.

edges.relationship: Parr uses Carson’s Silent Spring as an example of conveying nature’s active response and humans’ reciprocal relationship with it.
edges.evidence_note: Own 20 explicitly asks readers to consider how Carson’s depiction of active, responsive nature altered conceptions of biology, culture and environment. Parr uses this example within her argument for bodily environmental knowledge: a text can help urban readers recognize the reciprocity planters and gleaners knew through practice. This preserves the productive role of texts within her argument about embodiment; it does not claim personal contact, universal reception, or a fresh full reading of Silent Spring. The original book and absent notes 67–68 unread.

edges.relationship: Ouellet challenges Creighton’s national-bourgeoisie and social-decapitation account of the Conquest while identifying shared assumptions with later Quebec nationalist interpretations.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1984 survey 226–228 explicitly places Creighton before Séguin in connecting the Conquest with removal of a commercial bourgeoisie, then questions that class’s autonomy and its supposed harmony with the colonial metropolis. Ouellet proposes an Ancien Régime society dominated by military/landed nobility and clergy, and treats commercial dependence differently. He preserves differences among Creighton, Séguin, Frégault and Brunet, not an identical doctrine. At 228 he acknowledges revising his own earlier near-total social-continuity account concerning the Conquest’s negative political and military effects on the nobility; 229 credits Creighton among economic-social pioneers. This scoped disagreement coexists with Ouellet and Hamelin’s separate 1962 borrowing in edge 991. Original Creighton books and the other historians’ cited works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Davis contrasts Creighton’s emphasis on metropolitan elites with Careless’s ecological interdependence and questions the latter’s combination of elite agency with impersonal systems.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly reader Davis 1985:97–98 and 101–103 distinguishes several metropolitan approaches rather than one thesis. His comparison identifies Creighton’s entrepreneurship of central elites and Careless’s mutually dependent city–hinterland relations; it also criticizes Careless’s uneven combination of Laurentian elites with Gras’s ecological model. Crucially, at 101 and note 47 on 110 he reports Careless’s explicit denial that his original inspiration came from Creighton or Innis, crediting medieval communitas studies and Gras instead. The undirected comparison therefore records Davis’s interpretation, not a proved teacher–pupil lineage, personal endorsement or contradiction resolved in favor of one author. Careless’s cited private letter and original works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon trace Rodney’s early use of Fanon’s analysis of the national bourgeoisie when interpreting Tanzania’s socialist experiment.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly readers Chukwudinma and Kallon 2025 explicitly identify The Pitfalls of National Consciousness as Rodney’s frequently invoked resource during 1969–74 and afterwards. They quote his 1972 accounts of the dependent petty bourgeoisie and intelligentsia’s possible transformation, while distinguishing his terminology from Fanon’s and crediting Cabral for a class-suicide formulation Rodney associated with Fanon. The authors show later revision and continuing debt rather than an unchanging or exclusive lineage. This is their attributed analysis of quoted published and archival Rodney material; the original papers, full lectures and Fanon book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon identify Rodney’s later disagreements with Fanon over revolutionary organization and the class character of postcolonial African societies.
edges.evidence_note: The authors’ 2025 original article quotes Rodney’s 1973 Cabral eulogy and 1978 Hamburg distinction between violence itself and its political organization, then traces his post-1974 view of Tanzania’s bureaucracy as a ruling class rooted in production. They describe a move beyond the early model of a dependent stratum that might renounce privilege. Their account expressly calls Rodney’s portrayal of Fanon as an apostle of spontaneity a misreading, since Fanon also demanded organization; it also finds that Rodney retained some Fanonian hopes about guerrilla leadership. The disagreement is Rodney’s interpretation as mediated by these two readers, not a finding that Fanon simply ignored organization or a complete rejection of Fanon. Original eulogy, recordings, research papers and Fanon book unread. The existing James 401 criticism concerns a distinct retrospective assessment of Rodney.

edges.relationship: Harding, Hill and Strickland credit Wallerstein with helping organize Rodney’s lecture and teaching visits while he worked under repression in Guyana.
edges.evidence_note: The jointly authored introduction, copyright 1981 and reproduced in the actual licensed Verso 2026 preview, names Wallerstein at Binghamton and James Turner at Cornell as especially helpful in organizing opportunities for Rodney to lecture and teach abroad. It explains that these visits sustained contacts and earned money his family needed while he remained in Guyana. Both helpers retain credit. This is their specific retrospective testimony about practical scholarly support, not an inference that Wallerstein supervised Rodney or supplied his dependency theory. The preview ends within Walter’s Legacy and omits the introduction’s endnotes; no complete introduction, original 1981 pagination or full book read.
